data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Resumption safety depends on the distinction between budget-exhaustion halts and all other halt causes. Budget-exhaustion halts are resumable iff the event log maintains a monotonic, content-addressed identity chain (each event's ID is a hash of its content plus the prior event's ID) and the halt did not interrupt a write. Any halt caused by crash, power loss, or process kill\u2014rather than graceful budget exhaustion\u2014must be refused resumption pending a full integrity audit, because the causal mechanism of the halt differs.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The system claims graceful budget exhaustion but actually crashed due to OOM while checking the budget (mechanism mismatch).","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The content-addressed chain is valid but an event was silently dropped (valid chain over incomplete data).","eval":"observation"},{"case":"A crash occurred but the storage layer guarantees atomic writes (e.g., WAL with fsync), making the crash halt equivalent to a clean halt.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The budget-exhaustion halt path itself has a bug that can leave partial writes.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A content-addressed identity chain makes append-only integrity verifiable: tampering with any event breaks the chain. Graceful budget exhaustion is a controlled stop that can guarantee no in-progress write. Crash halts lack this guarantee because the process may have been mid-write. The distinction matters because the causal mechanism of the halt determines whether the log tail is a trusted boundary. Budget exhaustion is a planned stop; crashes are unplanned and require audit before trust can be restored.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
